comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text:
People on the Internets have problem with literally everything. As in - there are always some people who have problem with something.

You change a keybinding, or UX element in popular software and you'll get a small crusade of people who absolutely hate the change. You say anything on social media, you'll get a crowd arguing with it.

Negative emotions motivate people to speak out. Being satisfied much less so.

You just learn to shrug.

For all the whining, I know tens of developers who are absolutely thrilled and adapting at fast pace. And they typically are busy getting stuff done not posting stuff online.

Obviously LLMs are a severe and fast paced change, but it is what it is, and the world with adapt. And there's tons of nuance in it, not just all good or all bad. Even if it was all for the worse (which it isn't), I would rather adapt and do my best than weep.

comments.author: jzb
comments.text:
I think it's unfair, and a bit intellectually dishonest, to try to compare legitimate complaints about LLMs and their impacts with things like people complaining when an application changes keybindings or UX elements.

"People on the Internets have problem with literally everything. As in - there are always some people who have problem with something."

That does not mean that all criticism should be ignored. You have to be willing to evaluate criticism and decide whether it's an example of "you can't make everybody happy" or a legitimate problem. Hand-waving away people's objections about LLMs with the idea that some people are always unhappy is, IMO, a cop-out. I mean, using that logic to handwave away criticism, you can justify anything.

comments.author: dpc_pw
comments.text: I use trivial examples, just to drive the point that people are vocal and critical even about most trivial of things. So predictably they are going to be even more critical and dramatic about something that does have legitimate issues.

comments.author: jzb
comments.text: It's difficult to square "legitimate issues" with dismissive terms like "dramatic" and "whining". It seems your preference would be if people would just, you know, never speak up at all. That's unfortunate.

comments.author: hwayne
comments.text:
I am scared about how AI affects my economic prospects. I also know a doctor who never coded before, who used ChatGPT to make a customized shift trading platform at his hospital, which apparently significantly improved the lives of all the nurses.

Do our needs trump theirs? Is it better for software engineering to remain a high-salary, high prestige job, or for more nonengineers to be able to make situated software? I don't think it's a clear-cut answer, and I don't think that uncertainty speaks to a problem in my heart.

comments.author: mtset
comments.text:
Hillel, if it weren't you, I think I wouldn't reply to this at all. Since it is you, let me try to be as clear as possible about why I find this argument hard to take seriously and, frankly, a bit frustrating.

You've established a dichotomy here: either software engineers have excellent career prospects or ordinary people are empowered to create software. In doing so, you've set me in a position I didn't take: the gatekeeper.

I am all for the democratization of software engineering. I have spent my entire career doing technical writing, documentation work, and blogging on the side, trying to create on-ramps for people. In my personal life, I do the same in a more hands-on way.

I am also a socialist. I don't care about being wealthy; I care about the people in my community, including myself, being housed and fed. Show me a way to cut my salary by 80% that puts that money into social programs instead of the pockets of billionaires and I'll vote for you. I do not care about my ability to make six figures going forward.

But, also, I don't think I am going to lose my job. I'm senior enough that I could always become a manager, and I'm good enough with these godforsaken tools that I don't think I'll have to. To the extent that I'm worried about economic prospects, I'm worried about exactly those people I've spent time trying to empower - non-professionals, young professionals, junior engineers - and people working in the foundations of CS, PL, and software tools, where we already see less and less funding being allocated in favor of building bigger slop machines.

If we had a coding model that produced good results for people who weren't engineers and had none of the governance, centralization, bias, economic, or environmental concerns that Anthropic and OpenAI's products and practices create, I would be all for it. I like AI; I think it's cool. The way I got into Rust in 2016 was writing genetic algorithms, for goodness sake! (And yes, I have and will continue to evaluate the landscape of open weight models. I find them lacking.)

What I don't like is the centralization of power and the way these models are being welded by capital, and I think people in our field who constantly sing their praises online are partially responsible for making that a reality.
